title: Retire dead marketing words: be specific, show, name the cliché, or own it
summary: Jason Cohen argues that overused marketing phrases like "authentic," "powerful," "secure," and "the leading provider" have lost meaning through repetition and misuse. He offers four fixes for website and sales copy: use specific numbers, show proof instead of claiming, name the cliché out loud to earn credibility, or back a claim so completely that you own it.

principles.text: Repetition kills even powerful words. Once everyone uses a phrase, it stops persuading.
principles.quote: repetition of even powerful, wonderful phrases will kill them.

principles.text: If you have to say it, it's probably not true. Claims like "innovative" or "secure" get disproved by behavior.
principles.quote: if you have to say it, it's probably not true

principles.text: Replace vague adjectives with concrete numbers and facts, like requests processed daily or attacks blocked.
Show the product in action instead of describing it: speed tests, 60-second demos, changelogs, real unsolicited testimonials.
principles.quote: Instead of saying it's easy, have a video demonstrating your tool solving someone's problem in 60 seconds flat.

principles.text: Open a pitch by mocking typical pitches and saying the quiet part out loud. Candor earns credibility.
principles.quote: Because you're willing to say the quiet bit out loud, to say what others hide, especially when we all know the truth, you earn credibility.

principles.text: You can use a worn-out claim only if you own it completely with proof, and communicate that proof rather than leading with the phrase.
principles.quote: if you *lead* with the dead phrase I'll leave before you get the chance to prove it.
